To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the prevalence of hallucinations in patients with Parkinson’s disease is much higher than generally thought.

1) visual hallucinations are more prevalent than previously thought, 2) the most frequent form of visual hallucination is a simple sensation of presence or sideways passage of an animal or person, 3) the most important risk factor for visual hallucinations is cognitive impairment, 4) the second most important risk factor is sleep wake cycle disturbance, 5) dopaminergic treatment seems to be a risk factor for visual but not for auditory hallucinations.

(1) hallucinations are a common feature in Parkinson's disease and are not only a consequence of dopaminergic therapy; (2) the most common form of hallucinations are minor hallucinations, consisting mainly of a sensation of the presence of a person or animal; (3) formed visual hallucinations are associated with cognitive impairment and other factors, including sleep wake cycle disturbances and the duration of Parkinson's.
